title: What went wrong: Opus 5 ultracode wiped a production database

reading.body:
An AI coding agent connected to a production database with unrestricted credentials executed a command that wiped all tables. The agent was instructed to autonomously resolve database issues, and when it ran a Prisma migration command, it targeted the live production database instead of a test environment. Complete data loss occurred within about 10 minutes. The agent detected and reported the error to the developer, but this detection did not prevent the damage.

This is a failure of access control and deployment safeguards, not of the model's reasoning. The command syntax itself was not inherently destructive, so the agent had no way to flag it as dangerous based on appearance alone. The incident required two conditions to cause harm: the agent held unscoped credentials with broad database access, and nothing validated the command target before execution. Either restricting the agent to non-production environments only, or requiring human approval of commands that target production systems, would have prevented the data loss.

It is not established whether the developer was acting within the bounds of the model's intended use, whether they understood the risks they were creating, or what contractual or policy obligations governed the setup.

What went wrong: Opus 5 ultracode wiped a production database

summary:
In early August 2026, a developer connected Claude Opus 5 to a production Supabase database with unrestricted access and instructed the AI agent to autonomously resolve database issues. When executing a Prisma migration command, the agent mistakenly targeted the live production database instead of a disposable test database meant for that operation. The command reset all tables, resulting in complete data loss across the production environment within approximately 10 minutes. The agent detected the error and reported it to the developer before the developer noticed the problem themselves.

The incident occurred because the migration command's syntax was not inherently destructive, making it difficult to flag as dangerous based on appearance alone. The real risk stemmed from two factors: the command pointed to the wrong database target, and the agent held unscoped credentials with broad database access. The developer could have prevented this by implementing guardrails to validate command targets against security policy before execution, or by restricting the agent's database access to non-production environments only.
